1Executive Summary

SRK Consulting (Canada), Inc. and Paterson & Cooke prepared this report for Canada Nickel Co. under project AR-M2V4D, located in Timmins, Ontario, Canada. The study assessed the seismic hazard of the site Crawford and derived from that assessment the design earthquakes, the seismic design criteria for the tailings storage facilities and for conventional structures, and the dynamic properties and seismic coefficients of the slopes, together with the strong-motion records for the dynamic deformation analyses.

Probabilistic Seismic Hazard Assessment (PSHA). The probabilistic assessment quantifies the seismic hazard at each site as annual exceedance rates for specified ground-motion levels (Cornell, 1968; McGuire, 2004). It adopted the regional seismic source model CAN, with a logic tree comprising 6 branches, together with GMM logic trees for the active shallow crust (ASC), stable continental crust (SCC), subduction interface (SIF), SIS30, and SIS55 tectonic region types. The 10,000-year return period defines the Maximum Design Earthquake (MDE). Table 1.1 reports, for the site Crawford, the mean PGA by return period and site condition; on reference rock, VS30=760 m/s, the PGA of the MDE is 258 cm/s2.

Deterministic Seismic Hazard Assessment (DSHA). The deterministic assessment postulates, for each tectonic source capable of controlling the site demand, its maximum credible earthquake (MCE): the largest reasonably conceivable earthquake under the presently known tectonic framework (International Commission on Large Dams, 2016). The assessment postulated 2 scenarios with Mw from 4.5 to 6.5; the deterministic design spectrum MCE is their envelope. Table 1.1 reports, for the site Crawford, the PGA of the MCE and of the MCE (84%) by site condition; on reference rock, VS30=760 m/s, the PGA of the MCE is 232 cm/s2 and that of the MCE (84%) is 368 cm/s2.

Uncertainty Treatment. Epistemic uncertainty is represented through the logic trees of the source model and of the GMMs, and aleatory variability through the standard deviation of each ground-motion model; every spectrum is reported as its mean and its quantiles. Each deterministic scenario combines the equally weighted rupture variants, the GMM branches with their weights, and the record-to-record variability in a lognormal mixture. For the site Crawford, on reference rock, the 0.84 quantile of the PGA exceeds its mean by 39 % for the MDE and by 58 % for the MCE; Table 1.1 reports both statistics by site condition.

Site Response. The design ground motions are defined for the VS30 conditions evaluated at each site from the spectral demand at the surface. The design demands were evaluated for 7 site conditions, with VS30 from 180 to 1,500 m/s, by combining the direct logic-tree evaluation at each condition with the ST20 transformation of the demand at the reference condition of 760 m/s, conditioned on the PGA of the same realization. The mean PGA of the MDE is 265 to 308 cm/s2 across the site conditions. These results represent ergodic mean responses; a specific stratigraphic profile requires a separate site-response analysis. Table 1.1 reports, for each site and site condition, the probabilistic PGA together with the deterministic envelopes MCE and MCE (84%).

Seismic Record Selection. Ground-motion time histories provide the seismic input for the dynamic deformation analyses. A suite of 30 strong-motion records from 30 earthquakes and 5 databases was selected, with Mw 4.8 to 6.5 and epicentral distance Repi 1 to 263 km, and scaled by factors of 0.87 to 2.11 to the target spectrum defined for CFD at VS30 = 800 m/s. The suite-mean spectrum has a relative RMSE of 0.501 with respect to the target, and the ratio of the suite-mean PGA to the target PGA is 0.594. The delivered suite includes the time histories, intensity measures, spectra, and provenance metadata of the selected records.

Design Criteria for Tailings Storage Facilities. Seismic design for tailings storage facilities is based on a two-level performance framework: the Operating Basis Earthquake (OBE), associated with continued operation, and the Safety Evaluation Earthquake (SEE), associated with preventing a tailings release (International Commission on Large Dams, 2016; U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, 1995). The design earthquakes of the tailings storage facilities were evaluated under GISTM, CDA, and ANCOLD, for the consequence classes and the operation, closure, and post-closure lifecycle stages that each framework defines (Australian National Committee on Large Dams (ANCOLD), 2019; Canadian Dam Association (CDA), 2021; Global Tailings Review (ICMM, UNEP, PRI), 2020). On reference rock, the design PGA ranges from 8 to 361 cm/s2 across frameworks, consequence classes, and lifecycle stages. Table 1.2 reports, by consequence class and site condition, the design PGA of the GISTM framework at the operation stage; the design-criteria chapter reports the design PGA and design spectra by framework, consequence class, lifecycle stage, and site condition.

Design Criteria for Conventional Structures. Seismic design criteria for conventional structures were established from the hazard and site-response analyses in accordance with the site-specific procedure of ASCE/SEI 7-22, in which each MCER ordinate is the lesser of the risk-targeted probabilistic component and the code-prescribed deterministic component (Minimum Design Loads and Associated Criteria for Buildings and Other Structures, 2022). The MCER spectra and the design parameters were obtained for the 7 evaluated site conditions: SDS ranges from 0.09 to 0.14 g and SD1 from 0.02 to 0.05 g. Table 1.3 reports the design parameters by site and site condition.

Dynamic Properties of Slopes. The flexible sliding-block displacement models require the fundamental period of each potential sliding mass and the dynamic soil stiffness that determines it. The analyses considered 8 material scenarios over 5 slope geometries with heights between 27 and 135 m. The estimated fundamental period varies with the material class between 0.22 and 0.36 s in the lowest slope, and between 0.73 and 1.34 s in the highest one.

Newmark Permanent Displacements. The Newmark permanent displacement Dn quantifies the displacement induced by an earthquake and accumulated in the sliding mass and is the performance measure from which the seismic coefficients are derived. The Dn(ky) curves relate, for each combination of geometry, material, and design scenario, the yield acceleration ky to the expected permanent displacement; they were computed with the ensemble set of AM88, JB07, SR08, BT07, and BM19, with the reference magnitude assigned to each seismic demand and 300 realizations per demand and are read at the fractiles q=1−pe.

Performance-Based Seismic Coefficients. The horizontal pseudostatic coefficient kh is derived from the allowable permanent displacement Da of the potentially sliding mass (Bray & Travasarou, 2009; Macedo et al., 2018). The coefficients are reported at four relative displacement limits, Da/Hs = 0.1, 0.4, 1.0, 2.5%. Table 1.4 reports, for the MCE and the geometries analyzed, the range of the coefficient across the material scenarios at each limit, expressed as a percentage of the PGA.

The hazard curves, the probabilistic spectra, and the deterministic scenarios are presented in the Seismic Hazard Assessment annex. The selected records and their verifications are presented in the Seismic Record Selection annex. The design criteria and the structural design spectra are presented in the Seismic Design Criteria annex. The fundamental periods, the Newmark displacements, and the seismic coefficients are presented in the Ground-Motion Design Parameters annex.

2Introduction
2.1Objectives
The primary objectives of this study are as follows:

Seismic Hazard: Quantify annual exceedance probabilities for ground-motion intensity measures at the site using probabilistic seismic hazard analysis. Compute site-specific hazard curves and uniform hazard spectra at reference-rock conditions. Perform hazard deaggregation to identify controlling magnitude, distance, and epsilon (normalized residual) scenarios at each governing hazard level. Summarize the hazard results as mean and fractile annual-exceedance-probability curves for defined site conditions.

Site Response: Compute site-specific peak ground acceleration and spectral ordinates through two ergodic estimates — the direct evaluation of the ground-motion model tree, with each model’s own site terms, at each evaluated condition, and the transformation of the reference-rock motion through the Stewart and Hashash (2020) NGA-East ergodic amplification model — and combine their probability distributions as a finite mixture to define the design demand. Present the results as tables and figures summarizing peak ground acceleration and uniform hazard spectra for all evaluated site conditions and fractiles.

Slope Design: Quantify permanent slope displacements and derive performance-based horizontal seismic coefficients (kmax, kh) for slope stability design. Displacements are estimated using a weighted ensemble of rigid- and flexible-block Newmark models across all geometry classes, material scenarios, MDE and MCE demand scenarios, and allowable displacement thresholds. Seismic coefficients are determined by inversion of the displacement framework for each prescribed performance objective. Summarize the kmax and kh design values for all geometry–material–demand-scenario combinations.

Design Criteria: Establish seismic design criteria for tailings storage facilities based on international standards and consequence classification. Assign design earthquakes and performance objectives for all project lifecycle phases, including operation, closure, and post-closure, as required by GISTM, CDA, and ANCOLD. Determine Maximum Credible Earthquake (MCE) scenarios in accordance with regulatory requirements. Define the probabilistic design spectra and the associated ground motions for each operational stage and consequence rating. Establish, for conventional structures, the MCER spectra of the ASCE/SEI 7-22 (IBC 2024) site-specific procedure — the risk-targeted Maximum Considered Earthquake — and derive from them the design spectra, defined as two-thirds of the MCER ordinates, with their SDS and SD1 parameters.

Seismic Record Selection: Select, through magnitude and distance windows tied to the scenarios that control the hazard and with at most one record per event, a set of strong-motion records that represents the amplitude, duration, and frequency content of the seismic demand; process each horizontal component by removing the low-frequency mode associated with drift and noise and normalizing the energy of the reconstructed signal; scale the set to reproduce the mean of the site-specific target spectrum and to contain the individual spectra within its envelopes; and verify the resulting compatibility through the error of the spectral mean, the PGA ratio, and the contained fraction of ordinates, preserving the identification of events, stations, and intensity measures for the dynamic deformation analyses.

Uncertainty Modeling: Propagate epistemic uncertainty through logic-tree branching and aleatory variability through probabilistic integration across all analysis components. Propagate the hazard and model uncertainties in site response through analytical integration of the distributions to generate fractile site-response spectra. Aggregate uncertainties in ground-motion intensity measures, site response, and displacement models to generate fractile bands for Newmark displacements and performance-based seismic coefficients.

3Seismic Hazard Assessment
3.1Probabilistic Seismic Hazard Assessment (PSHA)

Probabilistic seismic hazard analysis (PSHA) quantifies the rate at which different levels of ground motion may be exceeded at the site. The assessment represents the range of magnitudes, locations, and ground motions through the seismic-source model and the ground-motion prediction models, and applies the total-probability theorem over the scenarios that can contribute to the demand (Cornell, 1968; McGuire, 2004).

The assessment adopted the regional source model CAN, with a logic tree comprising 6 branches, together with GMM trees for the ASC, SCC, SIF, SIS30, SIS55 regimes. The calculation domain begins at Mw 4.5, considers sources up to 1,000 km, and truncates the residual distribution of the GMMs at ±3.0σ.

Each seismic source contributes to the exceedance rate through its occurrence rate and through the magnitude and distance distributions of its earthquakes. For a seismic source s, ν0(s) is its annual occurrence rate above the minimum magnitude Mmin, m is the moment magnitude, and r gathers the source-to-site distance metrics required by the GMMs. The domain D comprises the admissible rupture locations and geometries for the source. The probability density functions (PDF) fM,s(m) and fR∣M,s(r∣m) describe the normalized magnitude and distance distributions of the earthquakes within source s, Mmax(s) is the upper magnitude bound of the source, I is the intensity measure, and i* the level whose exceedance is evaluated. With these definitions, the contribution of the source is
λI(i*)(s) = ν0(s)MminMmax(s)D​PI>i* | m,r fM,s(m) fR∣M,s(r∣m) dr dm(3.1)

This formulation is a direct application of the total-probability theorem in continuous form, integrating over all magnitudes and locations of earthquakes from source (s) that could contribute to exceedance of level i*. Aleatory variability represented in the recurrence, magnitude, location, and ground-motion models is propagated through the integration (Baker et al., 2021; McGuire, 2004).

The total hazard at the site sums the contributions of all the sources considered: if multiple seismic sources contribute to the hazard at the site, the total annual exceedance rate λI(i*) is obtained by summing the contributions from all sources,

Expression 3.2 assumes NS independent sources, each with its own occurrence rate and distributions, and evaluates λI(i*)(s) for each source through the hazard integral. This linear superposition is valid under the assumption that earthquake occurrences in different sources are independent, typically modeled as independent Poisson processes. The result is a seismic-hazard curve that quantifies the rate at which various ground-motion levels are exceeded at the site.

The term P[I>i*∣m,r] of the integral is supplied by the ground-motion model (Chapter 3.3), which enters PSHA through its median ηI and its total standard deviation σlnI. Variations among competing GMPEs in either quantity modify the exceedance rates, particularly at long return periods, where the integral weights the upper tail of the lognormal distribution (GEM Foundation, 2023).

The hazard curve is expressed as an annual rate, as a probability of exceedance over an exposure interval, and as a return period. The annual exceedance frequency λI(i*) obtained from the hazard integral 3.1 is the mean number of exceedances per year of level i*, and the curves labelled AEP in this report present that rate, in 1/year. If exceedances follow a Poisson process in time, the exact probability of at least one exceedance during a single year is

For small rates, P1yr≈λI, because e−λ≈1−λ. By extension, the probability of exceedance in T years is PT(I>i*)=1−exp[−λI(i*)T] under stationarity; this relation converts the mean annual rate into the probability for the exposure interval. The hazard integral propagates the aleatory variability of its models; the epistemic uncertainty of the models themselves is represented through the logic trees of the regional source model (Section 3.2.4) and of the GMMs (Chapter 3.3). Each branch specifies an alternative characterization with a non-negative weight, and the weights of each set sum to one. The recurrence, geometry, and maximum-magnitude parameters of each source enter the integral through the magnitude and distance densities. The GMM trees represent the active tectonic regimes separately and weight their prediction models; record-to-record aleatory variability remains in the standard deviation of each GMM. OpenQuake evaluates the hazard integral for the tree realizations and forms the requested statistics by weighting the resulting curves (Global Earthquake Model Foundation, 2024).

In this assessment, the assessment adopted the CAN model, whose logic tree comprises 6 branches; the GMM trees comprise ASC (4 branches), SCC (16 branches), SIF (4 branches), SIS30 (4 branches). The probabilistic output at reference rock (VS30=760 m/s) reports the mean and the 0.05, 0.1, 0.16, 0.5, 0.84, 0.9, 0.95 quantiles.

The PSHA aggregates the contributions of all plausible earthquake scenarios in the total exceedance rate, obscuring the specific combinations of magnitude (M), source-to-site distance (R), and ground-motion residual (ε) that control site hazard. Hazard disaggregation quantifies the relative contribution of each scenario class, binned by magnitude mk, distance rj, and residual εℓ, to the annual frequency of exceedance at a specified ground-motion threshold i* (Bazzurro & Cornell, 1999).

Disaggregation is performed at a target hazard level, defined by an annual exceedance probability or return period. This produces conditional probability distributions over scenario bins and identifies controlling scenario parameters responsible for site hazard (Kramer, 1997). The joint exceedance rate for scenario (mk,rj,εℓ) from source s is
ΔλI(i*,mk,rj,ε)(s)=1{ε≥ε*(mk,rj)} φ(ε) fM,s(mk) fR∣M,s(rj∣mk) ν0(s),(3.5)

where φ is the standard normal probability density function and 1⋅ is the indicator function; the ground-motion exceedance probability and the total annual exceedance rate that enter the formulation are those defined in the hazard analysis (see 3.1, 3.13). Integration over ε yields the two-dimensional (M-R) formulation. Partitioning parameter space into magnitude bins mk, distance bins rj, and residual bins εℓ, the contribution from bin (k,j,ℓ) is
λk,j,ℓ(i*)=s=1NSmk​rj​εℓ​ΔλI(i*,mk,rj,ε)(s)dε dr dm(3.6)

Hazard disaggregation applies Bayes’ theorem to the joint distribution of scenario parameters and ground-motion exceedance: the conditional probability that exceedance of i* is produced by this bin is
P[M=mk,R=rj,ε=εℓ∣I>i*]=θk,j,ℓ=λk,j,ℓ(i*)λI(i*)(3.7)
and the marginal probabilities are obtained by double summation over the other indices, over distance and residual for the magnitude,
PM∈mk∣I>i*=j​ℓ​θk,j,ℓ(3.8)
over magnitude and residual for the distance,
PR∈rj∣I>i*=k​ℓ​θk,j,ℓ(3.9)
and over magnitude and distance for the residual, whose marginal distribution quantifies the contribution of ground-motion residual bins to the exceedance:
Pε∈εℓ∣I>i*=k​j​θk,j,ℓ(3.10)

The modal scenario is the (k,j,ℓ) bin for which θk,j,ℓ of 3.7 attains its maximum. The mean scenario is the average magnitude–distance pair of the conditional distribution, weighted by those contributions.

In this report, the OpenQuake disaggregation outputs are presented as magnitude-distance (Mag_Dist) matrices. The calculation uses magnitude bins of 0.1 Mw, distance bins of 10 km, and the intensity measures PGA, Sa(0.10 s), Sa(0.20 s), Sa(0.50 s), and Sa(1.00 s). The reported heatmaps and modal table therefore summarize the two-dimensional M-R contribution surface for each selected return period and oscillator period. Disaggregation provides a data-driven basis for scenario selection in engineering analysis. The modal scenario and the highest-probability bins identified through disaggregation correspond to the earthquake characteristics most responsible for exceedance at the design ground-motion level.
3.1.1Hazard Curves and Spectra

AEP curves report the mean annual exceedance rate, λI, in 1/year for each ground-motion threshold. Total hazard curves integrate the contribution of all sources considered, and by-source curves retain the individual contribution. The exact probability for an exposure interval is presented in the PoE curves.

Probability of exceedance (PoE) curves report the probability that a specified ground-motion intensity is exceeded over the project exposure interval; under the Poisson process, that probability is converted from the mean annual exceedance rate of the AEP curves. The magnitude-distance disaggregation of each site, summarized by return period and oscillator period, closes the probabilistic assessment.

3.3Ground Motion Models (GMM)

The term P[I>i*∣m,r] in the hazard integral 3.1 represents the ground-motion model’s probabilistic prediction of exceedance and is obtained from ground-motion prediction equations (GMPEs). GMPEs are empirical or semi-empirical models that predict the statistical distribution of ground-motion intensity measures, such as PGA and spectral acceleration, given an earthquake’s characteristics. A GMPE typically provides a median predicted ground motion, often in log10 or natural-log units, as a function of parameters such as magnitude M, source-to-site distance R, and site condition, along with an estimate of aleatory variability, the standard deviation σ of the logarithmic residuals (Boore & Atkinson, 2008). A generic form of a GMPE for an arbitrary intensity measure I is given in 3.11, where F and S are indicator variables for fault type, such as reverse or normal, and site class, such as rock or soil, and ε is a standard-normal (zero-mean) random variable representing the random scatter, with σlnI being the log-standard deviation (Boore & Atkinson, 2008):
lnI≈ηI(m,r,F,S) + ε σlnI,(3.11)
If ηI(m,r,F,S) denotes the median intensity I (in linear units) for magnitude m at distance r and σlnI is the standard deviation of lnI, then the conditional exceedance probability is
where Φ is the standard-normal cumulative-distribution function and ε*, the number of standard deviations by which i* exceeds the median prediction for scenario (m,r,F,S), is
ε* = lni*−lnηI(m,r,F,S)σlnI(3.13)
The total aleatory standard deviation σlnI satisfies the quadrature relation

where τ is the between-event (inter-event) standard deviation and ϕ is the within-event (intra-event) standard deviation, both expressed in natural-log units. Under the mixed-effects decomposition adopted by most modern empirical GMPEs, the total residual for record j belonging to event i is partitioned as
εij=ηi+δij(3.15)

where ηi∼N(0,τ2) is the between-event residual for event i, representing systematic source-to-source variation not captured by the median functional form, and δij∼N(0,ϕ2) is the within-event residual for record j, representing path and site variability not resolved by the median prediction; the two residual components are assumed mutually independent. All three quantities σlnI, τ, and ϕ are period-dependent in most modern GMPEs and are tabulated or parameterized as part of the published model; non-ergodic formulations further partition τ and ϕ into site-specific and path-specific components, and the models of the adopted trees, documented in the Ground Motion Prediction Models appendix, are predominantly ergodic.

The predictor variables entering a GMPE vary by model and tectonic region type, but the following notation applies consistently across all models of the adopted trees. Moment magnitude Mw is the primary source-size parameter. Each model declares the distance metric it requires as part of its implementation. Site amplification is parameterized primarily by VS30, the time-averaged shear-wave velocity in the uppermost 30 m. Basin depth is captured by z1.0, the depth to the horizon where shear-wave velocity first reaches 1.0 km/s, and by z2.5, the depth to the 2.5 km/s horizon. Rupture geometry descriptors include ztor, the depth to the top of the rupture plane; the fault dip angle; the rake angle characterizing faulting style; the along-dip rupture width W; and hypocentral depth h. For subduction models, a binary backarc flag distinguishing forearc and backarc site positions is additionally required by certain implementations.

The ground-motion characterization adopts an independent logic tree for each tectonic region type present in the source model. The Ground Motion Prediction Models appendix documents, regime by regime, the branches that compose each tree – each one a ground-motion prediction equation (GMPE) with its weight – and the calibration context of each model.

GMMs are among the main contributors to the epistemic uncertainty of the PSHA, together with source-model components such as fault geometry, seismicity rates, and magnitude-frequency distributions. Unlike aleatory variability, epistemic uncertainty represents incomplete scientific knowledge of the true ground-motion process: it is in principle reducible with additional data and is represented through a discrete set of alternative models. In regions with scarce strong-motion records, the medians of candidate GMPEs can diverge substantially over the spectral periods and magnitude-distance ranges of engineering interest, and that dispersion is frequently the main contributor to the uncertainty band of the hazard curve at low exceedance rates; model uncertainty is therefore represented explicitly through a logic tree that samples the space of possible alternatives.

Each logic tree is defined for one tectonic region type and comprises a single branching level. Each branch specifies an alternative GMPE with a non-negative weight wk satisfying the normalization condition

where N is the number of branches in the set. The weights define a discrete probability distribution over the candidate GMPEs; when all models receive equal weight, wk=1/N, the tree represents a state of maximum model uncertainty, with no prior preference for any formulation. The tree is propagated by evaluating the hazard integral separately for each branch and combining the resulting curves with their weights (GEM Foundation, 2023), so that the mean hazard curve is the weighted average

where λI(k)(i*) is the annual exceedance rate calculated with the GMPE of branch k. The full distribution over branches also allows fractile hazard curves at prescribed probability levels, which characterize the dispersion originated by the GMM epistemic uncertainty.

The trees of this assessment assign equal weights to their branches, as their appendix sections detail. This weighting is a grounded epistemic response: where the strong-motion records are insufficient to discriminate statistically among candidate formulations, there is no empirical basis for assigning systematically greater weights to one model family, and differential weights would introduce an apparent precision without support, at the risk of under-representing the true range of epistemic uncertainty. From information theory, the uniform distribution is the maximum-entropy assignment under a state of equal prior knowledge (Motaghed et al., 2023).

The complement of that weighting is the breadth of the ensemble. A large set of diverse genealogies – European, New Zealand, Taiwanese, and global NGA-West2 calibrations in active crust; eastern North America and the European and Australian cratons in stable crust; regional databases from Chile, Japan, Taiwan, and Mexico together with the global NGA-Subduction compilation in the subduction regimes – spans the widest defensible range of predictions and reduces the risk that the mean curve be dominated by a narrow group of models sharing common assumptions or training data (U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission, 2012).

Comparisons among GMMs require an operation distinct from the combination of hazard curves. For a fixed cell x=(Mw,Repi,h,Tn,VS30), each branch k contributes a lognormal distribution with logarithmic median μk(x) and total logarithmic standard deviation σk(x). The cumulative distribution function of the weighted mixture is
FSa(a∣x)=k=1Nwk Φ​lna−μk(x)σk(x).(3.18)
and the tabulated quantiles are obtained by numerically inverting this function for the seven probability levels p of the products, 0.05, 0.10, 0.16, 0.50, 0.84, 0.90, and 0.95,
while the arithmetic mean of the mixture is evaluated directly from its lognormal components:
E[Sa∣x]=k=1Nwkexp​μk(x)+σk2(x)2.(3.20)

The separation among the branch medians represents the epistemic dispersion across models, and each σk retains the aleatory variability of its formulation; the p5–p95 band is bounded by the 5th and 95th percentiles of the mixed conditional distribution and gathers both contributions. This per-cell mixture is used in the attenuation curves, the comparative spectra, and the conditional scenario evaluations. In the PSHA, each branch is integrated separately before the hazard curves are weighted; the resulting uniform hazard spectra constitute the spectral input of the probabilistic estimation of Newmark displacements (Chapter 5.2), so the influence of the GMMs reaches that stage through those spectra (Verri Kozlowski, 2026a).

3.4Deterministic Seismic Hazard Assessment (DSHA)

The deterministic assessment characterizes the seismic demand through a finite set of postulated rupture scenarios. Each scenario represents the maximum credible earthquake (MCE) of one source: the largest earthquake reasonably conceivable along a recognized fault or within a geographically defined tectonic province, under the presently known tectonic framework (International Commission on Large Dams, 2016). Each scenario preserves the identity of the tectonic source, its tectonic regime, the adopted moment magnitude, the rupture geometry, and the source-to-site distances required by the ground-motion models. The objective is to obtain the conditional distribution of spectral acceleration for each scenario and to construct, period by period, the deterministic envelopes used in the comparison with the probabilistic hazard.

The construction of the scenarios starts from the tectonic characterization adopted for each source: tectonic regime, magnitude, and explicit geometric rupture variants. Each realization represents one of those variants, receives the same weight, and supplies the distance vector required by the ground-motion models. The logic tree corresponding to the tectonic regime (Chapter 3.3) supplies the model branches and their weights; each combination of rupture realization and GMM branch constitutes a component of the scenario distribution (GEM Foundation, 2023).

The two assessments differ in the treatment of the conditional exceedance probability: the probabilistic assessment integrates it over the recurrence of the sources, whereas the deterministic assessment computes that same probability conditioned on the occurrence of the postulated scenario. For the scenario e=(me,re,θe), me is the moment magnitude, re collects the source-to-site distances, and θe contains the remaining rupture parameters and the site condition. The intensity I represents the maximum horizontal ordinate Sa(Tn) at period Tn, and i* is the level whose exceedance is evaluated. Each component of the scenario distribution is a lognormal prediction. For a rupture realization r and a GMM branch g, the logarithm of the intensity is represented by a normal distribution with mean μrg=lnηI(me,rr,F,S), evaluated with the corresponding formulation, and standard deviation σrg=σlnI. In this expression, ηI is the median intensity in linear units, rr is the distance vector of the realization, F represents the faulting style, and S the site condition. The fractiles are obtained by numerical inversion of G(⋅∣e),
and the mean is computed directly from the lognormal components:

The calculation obtains seven fractiles and the mean for each scenario, and the evaluation is carried out analytically from (μk,σk,wk); the comparison in this chapter presents the mean of each scenario and retains the 84th percentile only in the MCE (84%) envelope. The ordinates correspond to the maximum horizontal component at 5% of critical damping and are evaluated at the reference condition Vref=760 m/s; the PGA corresponds to Tn=0. This condition provides the computational reference from which the site-response model derives the site conditions actually evaluated (Chapter 4.1).

The scenario spectra remain separate and preserve the physical identity of each source’s earthquake across the period range. The report nomenclature defines two envelopes over the scenario set E through a single construction: the per-period maximum of the scenario ordinates for the reported statistic. The upper-fractile envelope, reported as MCE (84%), is

a maximum over values that does not select a scenario. The mean envelope, reported as MCE, applies the same construction to the scenario means, so its ordinates likewise belong to no individual scenario, and neither envelope identifies a controlling magnitude–distance pair. The comparison with the probabilistic hazard superimposes the deterministic envelopes MCE and MCE (84%) on the available mean uniform-hazard spectra and uses the mean spectrum for TR=10,000 years as the comparison level at the selected periods.

The distribution of each scenario integrates three sources of uncertainty, two epistemic and one aleatory. Epistemic rupture uncertainty is represented by the explicit physical variants adopted for the hypocentral depth, the dip, the rupture style, and the plane orientation; the NR realizations receive the same weight 1/NR. Epistemic model uncertainty represents the differences among the GMM branches admitted for the tectonic regime of the scenario; each branch enters with the weight vg defined by the adopted logic tree. Aleatory variability represents the record-to-record dispersion for a fixed rupture realization and GMM branch, and in component k=(r,g) it is expressed through the logarithmic standard deviation σk of branch g, evaluated for realization r.

The mixture of 3.23 represents the three sources through its parameters. The combination wk=vg/NR simultaneously incorporates the rupture variation and the model weighting; the dispersion among the medians μk characterizes the two epistemic contributions, while each σk contributes the aleatory variability of its component. The resulting distribution is characterized through the fractiles of 3.24, and each component preserves the correspondence among the rupture geometry, the source-to-site distances, and the GMM branch that originated its prediction.

The results of the deterministic assessment correspond to the maximum horizontal component of Sa(Tn) at 5% of critical damping on reference rock, VS30=760 m/s. The mean is presented for each scenario; the MCE and the MCE (84%) are obtained through independent per-period maxima. The table presents the spectral ordinates of the scenarios and their MCE envelopes; the graphical superposition of those spectra and the available mean uniform-hazard spectra is provided in the online results identified at the beginning of this section. The governing scenario is identified separately for each period and statistic, and that identification represents the changes of controlling source along the spectrum, so each envelope preserves the identity of the scenario contributing its ordinate at each period.

3.5Seismic Record Selection

The time histories constitute the seismic demand used as input to the dynamic deformation analyses and represent simultaneously its amplitude, duration, and frequency content. PGA characterizes the peak amplitude; the significant duration, the number of cycles near the peak, and the distribution of energy across frequencies describe additional characteristics that contribute to the accumulated deformation of slopes and embankments of cohesionless materials (Bray & Travasarou, 2007; Kramer, 1997). Record selection establishes a suite of motions whose spectral demand is compatible with the target band, whose temporal characteristics remain available to the dynamic models, and whose source events, stations, and records are identified.

The selected motions must be compatible with the hazard controlling the site, with the adopted target spectrum, and with the response variables of the dynamic model, and must represent the relevant record-to-record variability (NEHRP Consultants Joint Venture, 2011). The candidate set is delimited by magnitude and source–site distance windows tied to the scenarios controlling the hazard, identified from the hazard model and its disaggregation; the selection criteria further comprise the tectonic environment, the site conditions, component availability, usable frequency content, and record quality (Baker & Cornell, 2006). Within that set, spectral shape is evaluated by agreement with the target demand over the period range of the analysis – not through a separate conditional-spectrum or epsilon-based rule – and at most one record per event is retained. The target spectrum corresponds to the design ordinate of the demand adopted for the site – the mean or a design fractile, per the demand – and the lower and upper envelopes to low and high fractiles of that same demand; the envelopes define the admissible range around the target for the matched suite. The grid includes Tn=0 as the PGA ordinate and the positive periods of the analysis. The evaluation retains the identifiers of the event, the station, the record, and the source network or database, together with the intensity measures used to characterize the suite. No additional filters are applied by tectonic environment or by station VS30.

Deterministic channel mapping classifies the three recorded directions into the canonical components H1, H2, and UP, and the rotation of the two horizontals to their principal axes defines H1 and H2, with the rotation angle recorded per record. Spectral matching and verification are performed on H1, so that the record table, the intensity measures, and the reported spectra correspond to a single definition of horizontal motion. The procedure does not modify the frequency content of the records to reproduce the target spectrum: the adjustment is limited to the amplitude of the retained modes and to one scale factor per record, so that each history preserves the phases, the sequence of cycles, and the non-stationarity of the recorded motion – the properties that contribute to the accumulated deformation of slopes and embankments – and the compatibility of the suite with the target band is achieved in the spectral mean and in the containment of the individual spectra.

Empirical mode decomposition introduced intrinsic mode functions as data-adaptive components for nonlinear and non-stationary time series (Huang et al., 1998). The adopted procedure uses variational mode decomposition (VMD), which represents a non-stationary signal as a set of modes with compact frequency bands and a residue (Dragomiretskiy & Zosso, 2014); the canonical histories of the full record are decomposed component by component. 4.1Site-Response

The design ground motions are defined for the VS30 conditions evaluated at the site from the spectral demand at the surface. The assessment represents these effects through two alternative estimates of the surface spectral demand and combines the corresponding probability distributions to define the design demand at each structural period, return period, and VS30 condition. The GMM logic tree is evaluated in the hazard model for the project VS30 conditions (180, 270, 360, 560, 800, 1250, 1500 m/s). Each model incorporates its empirical site term when estimating Sa(Tn,VS30); the logic-tree weights represent the adopted epistemic alternatives, and the aleatory variability of each model is integrated into the exceedance curves. The assessment therefore retains the same source and ground-motion characterization used in the rock assessment; the site terms are evaluated for each VS30 value analyzed. The GMM site term and the external model represent mean ergodic responses derived from sets of records.

The demand calculated for the reference condition Vref=760 m/s constitutes the input to the NGA-East ergodic site-amplification model (ST20), developed by Stewart et al. (2020) and Hashash et al. (2020). For each period Tn, condition VS30, and realization of the input PGA pga*, the factor F is modeled as a lognormal random variable whose natural logarithm has mean μlnF and standard deviation σlnF,

The resulting distribution is defined as a finite mixture of the two; its formulation and its statistics are presented in the uncertainty section.

The factor F of 4.4 follows the ergodic site-amplification framework developed for central and eastern North America. Stewart et al. (2020) establish the linear response and the reference-condition change; Hashash et al. (2020) formulate the intensity-dependent nonlinear modification. The model is expressed with respect to a 3000 m/s hard-rock condition. Its composite log-amplification f at a site condition VS30, for the oscillator period Tn and the input PGA pga*, is the sum of three components:
f(Tn,VS30,pga*)=lnF760(Tn,VS30)+lnFV(Tn,VS30)+lnFnl(Tn,VS30,pga*).(4.5)

To transform an input at Vref=760 m/s, the calculation applies the exact difference between the composite model evaluated at the target condition and at the reference condition, for the same period and input intensity:
μlnF(Tn,VS30,pga*)=f(Tn,VS30,pga*)−f(Tn,Vref,pga*).(4.6)

VS30 is the travel-time-averaged shear-wave velocity in the uppermost 30 m, Tn is the oscillator period, and pga* is the input PGA. In each evaluation of the composite model, Fcomp=F760FVFnl; the factor applied from 760 m/s is therefore the ratio between Fcomp at the target condition and at the reference condition. The linear term FV represents the stiffness change with respect to the reference condition and varies with VS30 and Tn; it equals unity at 760 m/s and decreases gradually toward stiffer conditions. The term F760 links the 760 m/s reference to the model’s native 3000 m/s hard rock; it depends on the period, generally exceeds unity, and weights reference profiles with impedance contrast and with velocity gradient. The difference in 4.6 preserves that weighting in both evaluations, including its transition for velocities below 600 m/s.

The term Fnl represents the variation of amplification with ground-motion intensity and depends on VS30, Tn, and the input PGA pga*. The formulation uses a period-dependent reference – 760 m/s for Tn<0.4 s and 3000 m/s for longer periods – and converts the input PGA at 760 m/s to the hard-rock reference through pga3000*=pga760*/2.275 (Hashash et al., 2020; Stewart et al., 2020). At low intensities the response approaches the linear regime; as pga* increases, the term reproduces the reduction in amplification associated with nonlinear soil response. The balance between FV and Fnl makes it possible to represent amplification at intermediate and long periods and reduction at short periods for softer soils, while the transformation approaches unity when the target condition coincides with the reference.

The dispersion of 4.2 accompanies the same evaluation by period, velocity, and intensity. σL represents the dispersion of the linear term; σI enters the conversion from the 3000 m/s reference and vanishes when the input is already expressed at 760 m/s; and σNL=σf2ln[(pga3000*+f3)/f3] represents the dispersion of the nonlinear term. The coefficients and the transitions with Tn and VS30 are those tabulated by Stewart et al. (2020).

The 760 and 3000 m/s references serve distinct roles in the calculation. The former corresponds to the B/C boundary of the NEHRP classification and is a customary reference condition in United States ground-motion models and design criteria; moreover, much of the recorded data supporting these models concentrates approximately between 200 and 800 m/s. The latter represents the shallow crystalline basement of central and eastern North America used by NGA-East and by regional hard-rock assessments. Stewart et al. (2020) establish the conversion between the two references while maintaining compatibility with the empirical data and the site classes. The model is calibrated primarily for VS30 between approximately 200 and 1500–2000 m/s and applies gradual transitions toward the limits of its domain.

4.2Seismic Design Criteria for Slopes

The seismic design of tailings storage facilities is based on the two-level performance framework consolidated by dam-safety practice: an Operating Basis Earthquake (OBE), which the facility must withstand without operational interruption, and a Safety Evaluation Earthquake (SEE), under which it must not release tailings. ICOLD Bulletin 148 formalizes this framework for embankment structures (Australian National Committee on Large Dams, 2012; International Commission on Large Dams, 2016), and the USACE Engineer Regulation ER 1110-2-1806 expresses it in terms of the OBE and the Maximum Design Earthquake (MDE) (U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, 1995).

Three international frameworks implement these two performance levels for tailings storage facilities according to the consequence class of the facility: the Global Industry Standard on Tailings Management (GISTM) (Global Tailings Review (ICMM, UNEP, PRI), 2020), the Canadian Dam Association (CDA) guidelines (Canadian Dam Association, 2019; Canadian Dam Association (CDA), 2021), and the Australian National Committee on Large Dams (ANCOLD) guidelines (Australian National Committee on Large Dams (ANCOLD), 2019). The consequence class, from Low to Extreme, reflects the potential severity of a failure in terms of population at risk, anticipated loss of life, and environmental and socio-economic impacts, governs the stringency of the seismic criteria, and sets progressively more stringent annual exceedance probabilities (AEPs) for the design earthquakes. GISTM defines five consequence classes, CDA five consequence classifications, and ANCOLD six consequence categories, with three gradations, High C, High B and High A, within its High category. The classes and the design-earthquake AEPs of each framework are tabulated in Tables 6.1, 6.2 and 6.3.

Each framework designates the design earthquake in its own terms. GISTM specifies a single design ground motion for each consequence class and lifecycle stage, with the Maximum Credible Earthquake (MCE) evaluated in parallel and governing whenever it produces the higher demand (2020). CDA adopts the SEE as the design basis, admits the MCE as a declared alternative to the probabilistic level for high-consequence facilities, and allows risk-based departures for lower classes during transitional closure stages provided the post-closure requirements are ultimately met; its tabulated levels are targets for initial consideration and consultation between owner and regulator, and the designer of record and the owner may adopt more stringent levels to further reduce risk, or less stringent ones where justified (2021). ANCOLD assigns an OBE and an SEE to each consequence category: a uniform OBE of 1/500 AEP together with an SEE that ranges from 1/1,000 AEP up to the greater of the MCE and the 1/10,000 AEP event (84th percentile) for the Extreme category (2019), in line with mining-sector regulatory guidance that assigns design return periods of 10,000 years or longer to extreme-consequence structures (Seismic Permanent Displacements for Tailings Storage Facilities and Waste Rock Dumps, n.d.).

For a given consequence class, the design earthquake also varies with the lifecycle stage. During construction, partial-height embankments are checked against the OBE as a minimum, and against the SEE for high-consequence facilities or in high-seismicity regions. During operation, the stage with the largest stored volumes and the highest risk profile, the differentiation by consequence class is greatest: operational AEPs range from 1/200 (GISTM, Low) or 1/100 (CDA) to 1/10,000 for Extreme facilities. Closure and post-closure criteria are specific to each framework. GISTM retains the operational criteria through active-care closure and sets a 1/10,000 AEP for all classes during passive-care post-closure (Global Tailings Review (ICMM, UNEP, PRI), 2020). CDA retains criteria that depend on the consequence classification through closure and passive care: closure under active care with regular monitoring retains the levels of the construction, operation and transition stages, and passive care, which is distinct from abandonment of the facility, begins only once a steady-state condition has been demonstrated by accumulated experience and monitoring; any risk-based transition must be justified (Canadian Dam Association, 2019; Canadian Dam Association (CDA), 2021). ANCOLD adopts for post-closure the SEE of the applicable category and requires it to be reassessed at closure when the hazard, the condition of the dam, or its consequences change (Australian National Committee on Large Dams (ANCOLD), 2019).

In this report, the MDE is represented by the probabilistic spectrum for a 10,000-year return period, whereas the MCE is represented by the deterministic envelope. GISTM requires comparison of the MDE and MCE for the Extreme class during operations and active-care closure, and for every class during passive-care post-closure (Global Tailings Review (ICMM, UNEP, PRI), 2020). For CDA, the alternative between the probabilistic level and the MCE is set against the MDE for the Extreme class during construction, operation, and transition, and for the Very High and Extreme classes during closure and passive care (Canadian Dam Association (CDA), 2021). ANCOLD assigns the MDE to the High A category and, for the Extreme category, requires the greater of the MDE and MCE (Australian National Committee on Large Dams (ANCOLD), 2019).

Design ground motions for slopes are reported by lifecycle stage: operation, closure, and post-closure. The design earthquake that applies to each stage, whether the OBE, the SEE, or the PCE, is the one that each standard assigns to the consequence class of the facility in Tables 6.1, 6.2, and 6.3: ANCOLD designates it as the OBE or the SEE of the consequence category, GISTM as the design ground motion of the class and stage, and CDA as the Earthquake Design Ground Motion (EDGM) of the consequence classification. For each site condition, the probabilistic demand of a criterion is derived by linking its prescribed return period to the available uniform hazard spectrum (UHS); where the criterion is defined between two return periods, the design demand is the average of the demands evaluated at both, and the UHS is taken at its mean, except for the ANCOLD Extreme-category closure criterion, which is taken at the 84th percentile. Where the Extreme-class criterion invokes the MCE, the MCE (mean) and MCE (84%) series accompany the design spectra. The design PGA and design spectra are reported by framework, consequence class, lifecycle stage, and site condition.

The verification of the slopes under those design earthquakes follows the practice that ICOLD and FEMA frame for dams and embankments through successive tiers of analysis including pseudostatic stability checks, simplified estimates of permanent deformation, and dynamic analyses where warranted by the consequences of failure, anticipated response, or complexity of the failure mechanism (Federal Emergency Management Agency, 2005; International Commission on Large Dams, 2016). Within this framework, the Newmark method provides a deformation-based assessment that complements the limit-equilibrium analysis. The pseudostatic seismic coefficient is a project-specific value rather than a universal value assigned to a particular structure type. USACE manuals EM 1110-2-1902 and EM 1110-2-2100 include pseudostatic analysis among the methods applicable to dams and earthworks and address the sliding block for estimating permanent seismic deformation. Selection of the coefficient considers the site-specific seismic hazard, potential failure mechanism, and project performance criteria, so the coefficient results from the conditions of each project instead of a single value applicable to all of them (U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, 2003, 2005).

Two further references relate the pseudostatic verification to the permanent deformation. NCHRP Report 611 formulates the seismic analysis of slopes and transportation infrastructure in terms of displacement-based performance and uses simplified Newmark correlations to relate demand to permanent deformation (Anderson et al., 2008), and Eurocode 8 ties the pseudostatic action to the design seismic acceleration and the consequence class and admits Newmark displacement calculations when the ratio between the critical acceleration and the design acceleration justifies a deformation-based verification (European Committee for Standardization, 2004). These references provide the framing and the comparison criteria for the coefficients of this report; their indicative values serve that comparison, and the displacement objective defined for the project governs the coefficients themselves.

That objective is expressed as an allowable permanent displacement relative to the slope height. This report evaluates the coefficients at four damage thresholds of the relative permanent displacement, Da/H = 0.1, 0.4, 1.0, 2.5%: the crest-settlement ratios derived from ninety case histories of earthquake damage to embankment dams and associated with the Operational, Damage, Life Safety and Collapse limit states of the Italian dam code NTD14 (Aliberti et al., 2019). Their denominator, the reference height, includes the embankment height and the thickness of the deformable foundation and is adopted here as the slope height for normalization. The seismic coefficient tables are presented for these four thresholds and the coefficient figures shade the intervals they delimit. Chapter 5.2 describes the derivation of the coefficients from the allowable displacement.

5.2Performance-Based Seismic Coefficient

Pseudostatic seismic design of slopes requires a horizontal coefficient representing earthquake loading on the sliding mass. In this report the coefficient is derived from displacement-based performance: the Newmark permanent displacement Dn is the slope-deformation performance measure, and the coefficient kmax is the lowest yield coefficient ky consistent with a performance objective defined by the allowable displacement Da and the target maximum probability pe that Dn exceeds Da. The normalized coefficient kh expresses kmax as a percentage of the site-condition PGA after site response is accounted for in each geometry–material combination, and the coefficients are reported by geometry, material and seismic demand. For the slopes considered, Dn is estimated probabilistically by combining empirical regression models within a lognormal framework.

The horizontal pseudostatic coefficient is derived in this assessment from the allowable permanent displacement Da of the potentially sliding mass (Bray & Travasarou, 2009; Macedo et al., 2018). The seismic demand and the fundamental periods established in the preceding chapters allow the Dn(ky) relations between the Newmark permanent displacement and the yield coefficient to be computed; their inversion yields kmax, and its normalization by the PGA transformed to the VS30 of each geometry–material combination yields kh, so that the result traceably links the deformation objective to the horizontal action employed in the stability verification. The yield acceleration ay represents the acceleration level that mobilizes the available resistance along the potential failure mechanism, and its dimensionless form is ky=ay/g; for each allowable displacement and target exceedance probability, the analysis determines the ky threshold that satisfies the performance criterion, and that threshold is kmax, the coefficient applied in the pseudostatic limit-equilibrium verification.

In the Newmark sliding-block method (Newmark, 1965), the potentially sliding wedge is represented as a rigid block resting on an inclined plane: relative motion begins when the driving acceleration exceeds the yield acceleration ay=kyg and continues until the relative velocity returns to zero, and the permanent displacement is the sum of those episodes over the duration of the earthquake motion, obtained by double integration of the acceleration excess. The extension of the procedure to dams and embankments (Makdisi & Seed, 1978) derived the equivalent acceleration of the sliding mass from its dynamic response and is the direct antecedent of the flexible formulations. The adopted empirical relations represent the accumulated displacement statistically through two idealizations: rigid-block models relate the displacement to measures of the base excitation, and flexible-block models additionally incorporate the dynamic response of the mass through Ts and the spectral acceleration evaluated at a period proportional to Ts.

The displacement calculation uses the seismic demand and the fundamental periods established in Chapter 5.1. For each geometry, material and seismic demand – the probabilistic spectrum of each evaluated return period and the MCE scenario – a joint sample of the intensity measures required by the rigid-block and flexible formulations is constructed; that sample is common to all models, so their differences represent the displacement formulation rather than incompatible seismic demands. Two inputs feed that sample. The probabilistic input for each return period is the reference-rock UHS, which for 10,000 years represents the MDE, and the MCE input is the rock spectrum of each scenario; both retain the complete distribution of the rock demand, and both are defined for VS30=Vref=760 m/s. For each geometry and material scenario, the spectral ordinates and the PGA are transformed to the corresponding VS30 through the ST20 amplification model (Hashash et al., 2020; Stewart et al., 2020).

At the site condition of each scenario, the joint sample comprises PGA, Sa(1.3Ts), and Sa(1.5Ts). The three measures are represented through empirical marginals in lnSa and a Gaussian copula with the full inter-period correlation matrix (Baker & Jayaram, 2008), and the samples are recentered to preserve the mean of each amplified marginal; in each realization, the three intensities remain paired, and each displacement formulation uses the measures entering its regression. The Arias intensity used by JB07 and SR08 completes the set of intensity measures; it is estimated for each realization from the PGA (Verri Kozlowski, 2023), and the relation is applied deterministically, so that each PGA realization determines a single value of IA and the displacement sample propagates the PGA variability.

For each scenario, 30 values of ky are evaluated, logarithmically spaced between 0.01 and max(PGA,0.80), where PGA is the mean site-condition PGA of the scenario. That interval establishes the computed range of the Dn(ky) relations, over which the formulations are evaluated and the inversion to kmax operates.

Each active formulation estimates the Newmark permanent displacement (1965) of the sliding mass from the yield acceleration and the intensity measures of its regression, and all of them express the positive displacement Dn, in centimeters, through
Dn=exp​μlnD+ϵσlnD,  ϵ∼N(0,1),(5.12)

where μlnD and σlnD are the mean and standard deviation of lnDn defined by each model, and ϵ is a standard-normal residual. Some source formulations contain a discrete branch of zero or negligible displacement; the implemented evaluation uses exclusively the positive lognormal branch. In every formulation, ky, PGA, and Sa are expressed in units of g – the acceleration of gravity – IA in m/s, and Ts in seconds; the Arias intensity is derived from the PGA of each realization according to 6.3, and the reference magnitude assigned to each seismic demand is applied to its geometry–material combinations. The published form of each formulation is reproduced in Appendix 6.5. The performance-based seismic coefficient is defined by
kmax(pe∣Da)=infky:P[Dn(ky)>Da]≤pe.(5.13)

where pe is the target probability that Dn exceeds Da: kmax is the smallest ky for which the probability of exceeding the allowable displacement is at most pe. The normalized coefficient, reported as a percentage of the PGA [% of PGA], is calculated using the site-condition PGA transformed to the VS30 of the geometry–material combination evaluated for each demand:
kh=100 kmaxPGA(VS30).(5.14)

kmax is expressed in units of g and kh as a percentage of the PGA of the corresponding site condition. These two quantities express the displacement criterion as the horizontal action of the pseudostatic verification.

The five formulations are evaluated individually and combined into the three sets that the tables and figures identify as IDn: rigid, flexible and ensemble. The displacement model provides individual realizations for AM88, JB07, SR08, BT07, and a fifth formulation selected by the tectonic context: BM17 for projects with subduction control and BM19 for projects with shallow crustal control. The overall design set, identified as ensemble, combines AM88, JB07, SR08, BT07, and the active BM branch with equal weights; the rigid family combines AM88, JB07, and SR08, and the flexible family combines BT07 and the active BM branch. The rigid family thus relates the displacement to measures of the base excitation, the flexible family additionally incorporates the dynamic response of the sliding mass through Ts, and the ensemble is the design set that combines both. For each ky, the displacements of a family are summarized from the weighted empirical distribution of the realizations of its models.

All models receive the same joint sample of PGA and spectral accelerations, and a single realization of ϵ is shared across the models and across all values of ky; each formulation scales that residual through its own σlnD, and the sampled PGA is retained with each realization so that the inversion preserves the pairing between displacement and seismic demand. The realizations of Dn are calculated for each material class with its mean dynamic properties; the fractiles of the stiffness profiles and of Ts are reported in Chapter 5.1 and are not propagated as additional realizations in the displacement calculation, and each material class is kept as a separate scenario through the inversion to kmax, so the displacement curves are not averaged across materials before that operation.

For each model and realization, the computed Dn(ky) relation is projected onto a non-increasing curve and inverted in the (lnDn,lnky) plane to solve the criterion of 5.13; when Da falls outside the calculated range, the relation is extrapolated in that plane from the two points at the corresponding end, with the single exception of the AM88 limit treated in Appendix 6.5. The inversion is performed first for each model within each realization. The root distributions of the models are then combined with the family weights and summarized through the arithmetic mean and the empirical fractiles q=0.05, 0.10, 0.16, 0.50, 0.84, 0.90, and 0.95 (Verri Kozlowski, 2026a). Because of the decreasing relation between Dn and ky, the fractile associated with the exceedance target satisfies expression 5.15, where q=0.84 corresponds to an exceedance probability of pe=16%.

The q fractiles are therefore the statistics associated with the criterion expressed through pe; the arithmetic mean summarizes the center of the simulated distribution and does not represent a target probability. The evaluation uses 300 realizations for each demand – the probabilistic spectrum of each return period TR = 100, 200, 500, 1,000, 2,000, 2,500, 5,000, 10,000 years and the MCE – and a grid of allowable displacements Da ranging from 1.35 to 337.50 cm. This grid contains, for every slope height, the damage thresholds Da/H = 0.1, 0.4, 1.0, 2.5% of Chapter 4.2, at which the coefficient tables are reported and which the coefficient figures shade; values of Da that exceed the calculated range of a realization are obtained through the logarithmic extrapolation defined above.

The Newmark displacements were computed with the ensemble set of five formulations: AM88, JB07, and SR08 for the rigid block, and BT07 and BM19 for the flexible block, BM19 being the branch for projects with crustal control, with equal weights. Every formulation received the reference magnitude assigned to each seismic demand and the demand of each of the 8 return periods, 100, 200, 500, 1,000, 2,000, 2,500, 5,000, and 10,000 years, and of the MCE, with 300 realizations per demand, over the 5 slope heights from 27 to 135 m, the 8 material classes, and the relative displacement grid Da/Hs = 0.05, 0.10, 0.25, 0.40, 0.50, 1.00, and 2.50 %.

The reference magnitudes assigned to the seismic demands were Mw = 5.5 for TR = 100, 200, 500, 1,000, 2,000, and 2,500 years; Mw = 6.5 for TR = 5,000 and 10,000 years and the MCE. Within each demand, the same magnitude was used for the geometry–material combinations.

6.2Ground Motion Prediction Equations (GMPE)
6.2.1Active Shallow Crust (ASC)

The Active Shallow Crust (ASC) ground-motion logic tree applies to all sources classified as the Active Shallow Crust tectonic region type. The tree comprises eight branches, each assigned equal weight wk=0.12500, with the total weight summing to exactly 1.00000. The uniform weighting reflects the equal epistemic standing afforded to all eight GMPEs; the supporting documentation does not provide explicit per-model selection rationale beyond ASC regime applicability.
The eight branches are documented below, with their assigned weight and calibration context:

AristeidouEtAl2024 (weight: 0.12500). A GMPE for active shallow crustal earthquakes developed using an artificial neural network regression on strong-motion data (Aristeidou et al., 2024). The model is calibrated for the ASC regime with records from events of Mw≥4.5.

Atkinson2022Crust (weight: 0.12500). A backbone crustal GMPE developed by Atkinson (2022) for the 2022 Aotearoa New Zealand National Seismic Hazard Model (NZ22), applying an equivalent point-source framework calibrated against New Zealand strong-motion observations spanning approximately Mw 4.0 to 8.0 at rupture distances up to approximately 400 km (Atkinson, 2022; Bradley et al., 2022). The model is calibrated specifically for the New Zealand crustal (ASC) setting.

BooreEtAl2020 (weight: 0.12500). The GMPE by Boore et al. (2021) for active shallow crustal earthquakes in Greece, published in the Bulletin of the Seismological Society of America, which adapts a global NGA-West2-family model to the faster attenuation and weaker magnitude scaling observed in Greek strong motions.

CampbellBozorgnia2019 (weight: 0.12500). The Campbell-Bozorgnia NGA-West2 model, implemented in OpenQuake via the campbell_bozorgnia_2014.py module and representing a 2019 update to the 2014 NGA-West2 CB model (Campbell & Bozorgnia, 2014). The model is calibrated for active shallow crustal earthquakes using the NGA-West2 database, covering approximately Mw 3.3 to 8.5 at distances up to 300 km.

ChaoEtAl2020Asc (weight: 0.12500). The active shallow crustal variant of a horizontal ground-motion model for Taiwan developed by Chao et al. (2020) (Chao et al., 2020), calibrated from a Taiwan strong-motion flat-file of more than 40,000 recordings spanning 1992 to 2016 using a two-step maximum-likelihood regression procedure. The model is calibrated for the Taiwan crustal regime.

KothaEtAl2020 (weight: 0.12500). The backbone GMPE by Kotha et al. (2020) for active shallow crustal earthquakes in Europe, published in the Bulletin of Earthquake Engineering (Kotha et al., 2020), serving as the ASC component of the 2020 European Seismic Hazard Model (ESHM20). The model was calibrated from the Engineering Strong Motion (ESM) dataset comprising 23,014 recordings from 2,179 earthquakes predominantly in Italy, Turkey, and Greece, spanning Mw 3.0 to 7.4 and Joyner-Boore distances from 0 to approximately 300 km. A hinge magnitude Mh=6.2 separates quadratic from linear magnitude scaling.

PhungEtAl2020Asc (weight: 0.12500). The active shallow crustal variant of a GMPE by Phung et al. (2020) (Phung et al., 2020), calibrated from the Taiwan strong-motion database using 13,415 ground-motion records from 187 crustal events. The model adopts a functional form based on Chiou and Youngs (2014) with Taiwan-specific recalibration and spans approximately Mw 3.5 to 8.0.

Stafford2022 (weight: 0.12500). A backbone crustal GMPE developed by Stafford (2022) for the 2022 New Zealand National Seismic Hazard Model as part of the NZ22 model set (Bradley et al., 2022), derived through adjustments to the Chiou and Youngs (2014) response spectral model. The model is calibrated for the New Zealand ASC setting, spanning Mw 4.5 to 8.4 at rupture distances from 0 to approximately 300 km.
6.2.2Stable Continental Crust (SCC)

The Stable Continental Crust (SCC) ground-motion logic tree applies to all sources classified as the Stable Continental Crust tectonic region type. The tree comprises six branches with a quasi-uniform weighting scheme: five branches each carry a weight of 0.16667 and the sixth (CollapsedNGAEastUSGS) carries the complementary residual weight of 0.16665, ensuring the total sums to exactly 1.00000. The SCC tree does not achieve exact uniform weighting, owing to the rounding required by the six-branch structure. The SCC tree contains fewer branches than the ASC, SIF, and SIS trees, reflecting the more limited number of GMPEs calibrated directly for stable continental regions.
The six branches are documented below, with their assigned weight and calibration context:

Atkinson2008prime (weight: 0.16667). This is OpenQuake’s implementation of the Atkinson referenced empirical relation for Eastern North America with the adjustment published by Atkinson and Boore (2011). The model applies to the stable continental regime.

AtkinsonBoore2006Modified2011 (weight: 0.16667). The Atkinson and Boore (2006) stochastic-based GMPE for Eastern North America (Atkinson & Boore, 2006), subsequently modified in 2011 to incorporate magnitude-dependent stress-drop scaling that improved agreement with newer observational data. A hybrid empirical GMPE for Central and Eastern North America (CENA) by Pezeshk, Zandieh, and Tavakoli (2011), published in the Bulletin of the Seismological Society of America (Pezeshk et al., 2011). ESHM20Craton (weight: 0.16667). The craton-specific GMPE developed by Weatherill and Cotton (2020) for the 2020 European Seismic Hazard Model (ESHM20), published in the Bulletin of Earthquake Engineering (Weatherill & Cotton, 2020). 6.4Site Classification and Ground Properties
6.4.1Site Classification

The seismic site condition is initially characterized by VS30, the time-averaged shear-wave velocity of the uppermost 30 m of the profile. The VS profile is obtained through geophysical investigations appropriate to the project conditions, among them borehole logging, seismic cone penetration tests, and surface-wave methods. The definition of VS30 preserves the shear-wave travel time through the layered profile:

where Hi and VS,i are, respectively, the thickness in meters and the shear-wave velocity of layer i within the uppermost 30 m, and N is the number of layers of the profile within that thickness. The expression corresponds to a travel-time average and provides the uniform velocity that reproduces the propagation time of the actual profile. VS30 is the site-condition predictor used by the ground-motion models and by the amplification relations of this assessment (Borcherdt, 2012). It also identifies the reference condition from which the hazard spectra and the rock-to-site transformations are interpreted. In the site-specific analyses, the calculation additionally uses the properties required by the response model; the initial classification does not replace that characterization. The parameter summarizes the average shallow stiffness, but it does not by itself describe stratigraphic contrasts, depth to bedrock, basin effects, or resonance periods. These limitations are considered when defining the scope of a site-specific evaluation and when interpreting the resulting spectral demand.

The NEHRP provisions classify sites into Classes A through E and reserve Class F for conditions requiring site-specific evaluation (Building Seismic Safety Council, 2015). The reference ranges based on VS30 are the following:
Class A: hard rock, with VS30>1500 m/s.
Class B: rock, with VS30 between 760 and 1500 m/s.
Class C: very dense soil or soft rock, with VS30 between 360 and 760 m/s.
Class D: stiff soil, with VS30 between 180 and 360 m/s.
Class E: soft soil, with VS30<180 m/s.
Class F: profiles requiring site-specific evaluation, among them soils susceptible to liquefaction or collapse, peats, organic clays, thick high-plasticity clays, and very soft clays.

Where velocity measurements are available, VS30 is the primary criterion. The provisions also include criteria based on penetration resistance and on undrained shear strength where the geophysical information is insufficient. Class F is not assigned through a single VS30 range and leads to a site response analysis in lieu of the direct application of generic factors.

ASCE/SEI 7-22 updates the discretization of site conditions and distinguishes Classes A, B, BC, C, CD, D, DE, and E through velocity ranges, from competent rock to soft soils (Minimum Design Loads and Associated Criteria for Buildings and Other Structures, 2022). Class F identifies conditions that require site-specific response procedures and is not assigned solely through a VS30 range. The ranges and descriptions of the adopted classification are presented below. The evaluated VS30 values represent the site conditions for which the demand is determined. The class of a particular location is assigned from the applicable geotechnical profile and from the additional conditions defined by the standard.

The evaluated site conditions extend down to VS30=180 m/s, which falls within Class DE; the assessment does not reach Class E. Softer conditions are reserved for site-specific response procedures: Class F requires them under ASCE/SEI 7-22 (Minimum Design Loads and Associated Criteria for Buildings and Other Structures, 2022, Sections 11.4.7, 21.1), and Class E may additionally be assigned through the soft-clay criterion of Section 20.2.2, independently of VS30. The ergodic amplification model declares its applicability for VS30 between 200 and 3000 m/s, and its authors recommend a site-specific response analysis for conditions with VS30 below 200 m/s (Hashash et al., 2020; Stewart et al., 2020). For profiles softer than those evaluated, the spectra and parameters of this report are not applicable without a site-specific response evaluation.
